questions.q: What was the status of the '22 rules' when Emma Coats tweeted them?
choices: Her own notes on lessons learned from colleagues
questions.explain: She later said she wished she'd called them guidelines.

questions.q: Where did the story spine originate?
questions.explain: Adams developed it in the late 1980s as a tool for building stories live on stage.

questions.q: A writer's spine reads: 'One day… And then… And then… Until finally…'. What's wrong?
choices: The events follow each other but don't cause each other
questions.explain: 'Because of that' forces causality, Aristotle's 'because of, not after'.

questions.q: Which spine line plays the role of the inciting incident?
questions.explain: 'One day' breaks the routine established by 'Every day'.

questions.q: According to the rules, which coincidence is acceptable?
choices: One that gets the hero into trouble
One that gets the hero out of trouble
questions.explain: Coincidences that rescue characters feel like cheating, because the escape isn't earned.

questions.q: Rule #1 says you admire a character more for…
questions.explain: Effort is sympathetic; success alone isn't.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of the story spine?
choices: It can't handle cause and effect
It guarantees causality but not surprise, theme or depth
questions.explain: A spine can be perfectly linked and still dull.

ideas: A story can be built from sentence starters: once upon a time, every day, one day, because of that, until finally.
Coincidences that get characters into trouble are fine; coincidences that get them out are cheating.
You admire a character for trying more than for succeeding.
